plan.angle: Hook: 'The benefit isn't only on the scale.' In 333,687 US veterans with type 2 diabetes (BMJ Medicine, 2026), staying on a GLP-1 was linked to about 18% lower risk of heart attack, stroke or death compared with people on an older diabetes drug (sulfonylureas). Stopping and later restarting was linked to about 12% lower risk vs the same group. On screen, under the numbers: 'vs sulfonylurea users · observational · veterans with T2D'. Line: 'Why people stopped wasn't random: cost, side effects, illness can all play a role.' Close: 'Planning any change? Do it with your prescriber.' Then the exact prescriber line and a pointer to the full video. 35–50s. Title suggestion: 'Staying on a GLP-1: 18% vs 12% Heart-Risk Gap in 333,687 Veterans #shorts'

plan.why: Spin-off of L1: a concrete-number hook that drives traffic to the long video while the story peaks over the next 3–7 days. | fact-check: The angle frames the numbers wrongly. The paper reports 18% lower risk (continuous use) and 12% lower risk (stop then restart), and both are compared with veterans on sulfonylureas, not with each other or with no treatment. 'About 18% vs about 12% for people who restarted' is only accurate with that qualifier. The working title 'The Heart Number Nobody Mentions' is a false/clickbait claim: the study got wide coverage. Sample: 333,687 analysed. Journal: BMJ Medicine, March 2026.

The GLP-1 benefit isn't only on the scale.

A study followed 333,687 US veterans with type 2 diabetes, all compared with users of an older diabetes drug (sulfonylureas):

→ Stayed on a GLP-1 the full 3 years: ~18% lower relative risk of heart attack, stroke or death from any cause — roughly 4 fewer events per 100 people over 3 years
→ Paused then restarted within 3 years: ~12% lower relative risk — roughly 2 fewer events per 100

script.working_title: Staying on a GLP-1 vs Restarting: 18% vs 12% Lower Relative Risk of Heart Attack, Stroke or Death vs an Older Drug in 333,687 Veterans #shorts
script.hook_pattern: Reframe hook ("the benefit isn't only on the scale"), then a concrete sourced number (333,687 veterans). Three results follow, all against the same sulfonylurea comparison group. Staying on for the full three years comes first, with its absolute number. Pausing and restarting comes second, also with its absolute number. Stopping for good (no clear difference) pays off the 'stopping' promise. An honest caveat covers why people stopped and who was studied, then the prescriber line. The last line loops back to the opening hook.

factcheck.summary: I checked both sources and they are real. The BMJ Medicine paper (Xie, Choi, Al-Aly; VA St Louis and WashU; March 2026) supports every number in the script: 333,687 analyzed (132,551 GLP-1 users and 201,136 sulfonylurea users), and MACE defined as heart attack, stroke or death from any cause. Continuous use vs sulfonylureas had an HR of 0.82, which is 18% lower. The absolute risk reduction was 3.76 per 100 over 3 years, so "roughly 4 fewer per 100" is right. Interrupted use had an HR of 0.88 (12% lower). The population was about 91% male with a mean age of about 66, so "mostly older men" is accurate. The WashU press release names cost, side effects and shortages as reasons people stop. The framing is careful: it says relative risk, names the comparison group, includes an absolute number, and calls it observational, "a link, not proof." The prescriber line is exact, and there's no dosing or stopping advice. Only minor wording improvements remain.

issues.claim: Staying on a GLP-1 was linked to about 18% lower relative risk
issues.problem: The 18% applies only to people who stayed on the medicine continuously for the full 3-year follow-up. As written, 'staying on' could be read as any length of use. The press release notes that use under about 18 months showed no significant benefit.
issues.fix: Staying on a GLP-1 for the full three years was linked to about 18% lower relative risk of heart attack, stroke or death from any cause. That's roughly 4 fewer events per 100 people over three years.

issues.claim: About 12% lower, against that same sulfonylurea group.
issues.problem: The absolute number is given for the 18% figure but not the 12% one. The paper reports 2.41 fewer per 100 over 3 years. Giving both keeps the comparison like-for-like, as the craft notes ask.
issues.fix: Narration: "Now the second group. Pausing, then restarting within those three years? About 12% lower, against that same sulfonylurea group. Roughly 2 fewer events per 100." stat_label: "vs sulfonylurea users · ~2 fewer per 100 over 3 yrs · observational · veterans with T2D"

issues.location: s4/s5 (scope vs working title and keyword 'stopping')
issues.claim: The Short covers staying on vs pausing and restarting.
issues.problem: The target keyword and the CTA title are about stopping, but the Short never says what happened to people who stopped without restarting. In the paper that group's HR was 0.96 (95% CI 0.92–1.01), not a significant difference from sulfonylureas. Adding it would pay off the 'stopping' promise, stated as an association, not a cause.
issues.fix: Optionally add to s4: "Stopping for good? No clear difference from the older drug." Keep it as an association and follow it with the s5 caveat.
